author: Errington
name_in_asr: Nagarahara (modern Nangarhar); Begram / Dasht of Begram
asr_identification: Masson: the Dasht of Begram, the plain of tumuli W of Jalalabad (Nangarhar, Afghanistan); Simpson 1881: further NW, on the survival of the name in Naghrat and Nagara Ghundi; Kyoto survey 1965 (Mizuno 1970–1): further W again, taking in the Ashrak Burj, the mounds and Chahar Bagh
evidence: Errington sets out three placings of Xuanzang's city without choosing: Masson's Begram, 'a mile and half or two miles' W of Jalalabad, a plain of tumuli with coins occasionally found (Masson 1841, p. 99, Topes pl. I); Simpson's (1881, pp. 190–1) map, which puts the city further NW on the name evidence of Naghrat and Nagara Ghundi rather than on the spread of mounds and surface finds, and marks Masson's Begram only as 'ruins – stones in heaps'; and the 1965 Kyoto survey, which puts it further W still, excluding Simpson's 'rock' but including the Ashrak Burj, the mounds and Chahar Bagh (Mizuno 1970–1, fig. 24). No excavation of the city site.
quote: Begram is identified as the city of ancient Nagarahara from … Masson (1841, p. 99, Topes pl. I) identifies the city with … the ‘Dasht of Begram [which had] numerous tumuli … 190–1) locates Nagarahara not by the spread of mounds and … 1965 survey locates Nagarahara still further west to exclude
note: Agrees with Mizutani and the study (the Begram plain W/SW of Jalalabad; which mound open). Shows that the Kyoto survey's city (Mizuno 1970–1, fig. 24, the source of Kuwayama's Shāh Naṣr Ghundai) lies W of both Masson's Begram and Simpson's site; Simpson's placing rests on a name echo only. No new site evidence.

author: Errington
name_in_asr: Tepe Ashrak / Burj Ashrak / Burj Jemadar / Mound of Shah Nasr / Dasht-i Bagram
asr_identification: Tepe Ashrak (= Mound of Shah Nasr), a little N of Chahar Bagh across the Sultanpur ravine, Dasht-i Bagram, W of Jalalabad (Ball and Gardin no. 261: 34°26′N 70°25′E): Xuanzang's c. 9 m stupa inside the city (Mizuno, tentative)
evidence: Mizuno (1970–1, pp. 112–13, fig. 24) tentatively identifies Xuanzang's 9 m stupa within the city with Tepe Ashrak. Errington's site entry gives the mound's names as Tepe Ashrak / Burj Ashrak / Burj Jemadar / Tupper Ashuk / Mound of Shah Nasr / Dasht-i Bagram: a large mound, by Masson 'evidently the base of a tope or ... a tumulus', with a later square tower on it, 'a little north of Chahar Bagh'; Masson thought it led to 'the site which may have been the chief city of this country at the period when the topes were erected'. Not excavated; photographed by the Kyoto team in 1965.
quote: Mizuno (1970–1, pp. 112–13, fig. 24) tentatively identifies … Xuanzang’s 9m high stupa with Tepe Ashrak and the … Ashuk/Ashruk / Mound of Shah Nasr / Dasht-i … remarkable of these is one called Tepe Ashrak, a little north of … Chahar Bagh, being separated therefrom by a broad and deep
note: Refines the study's open choice for the city: Kuwayama's Shāh Naṣr Ghundai is the mound Masson called Tepe Ashrak (Errington's synonymy), and Mizuno, on whose survey Kuwayama relies, put inside the city the 9 m stupa Xuanzang saw there; so the Kyoto proposal places the city round this mound N of Chahar Bagh. Tentative, unexcavated; Mizutani's area. Does not move the identification.

author: Errington
name_in_asr: Ashoka stupa (Dīpaṇkara jātaka); Tepe Khwaja Lahori / Tappa Khwaja Lahoree / Tupper Khwajeh Lahore
asr_identification: Tepe Khwaja Lahori, near the Kabul river on the skirt of the Begram plain W of Jalalabad (Ball and Gardin no. 1169: 34°27′N 70°23′E) (Mizuno, tentative)
evidence: Mizuno (1970–1, pp. 112–13) tentatively identifies the Aśoka stupa of the Dīpaṅkara jātaka, 2 li E of the city, with Tepe Khwaja Lahori: by Masson 'one of the most extraordinary objects on the plain of Jalalabad', base circumference 1800 ft (548.6 m), masonry parapets in diaper work, caves in its sides, coins, trinkets and funeral jars found on it (Masson read it as sepulchral); the Kyoto team photographed it with 'annex stupas' in 1965. Errington herself notes that the Aśokan attribution 'has not been verified on the ground'.
quote: Ashoka stupa with Tepe Khwaja Lahori … This mound is one of the most extraordinary objects on the … plain of Jalalabad, from its huge dimensions. Its base has a … circumference of 1800 feet [548.64m]; it stands near the Kabul … (near Jalalabad) commemorating the site of the Dīpaṇkara … not been verified on the ground
note: A third candidate for the study's open 02.03.02 (besides Ahin-Posh and Watters' Nagara Goondee): Mizuno's Tepe Khwaja Lahori, unexcavated. On Ball and Gardin's rounded coordinates it lies W/NW of Tepe Ashrak, Mizuno's in-city stupa (70°23′ against 70°25′E), which sits ill with a stupa 2 li E of the city; the minute-level coordinates may be too coarse to decide. Leaves the place open.

author: Errington
asr_identification: Nagara Ghundi stupa, SE of Tepe Khwaja Lahori, Jalalabad plain (Ball and Gardin no. 756: 34°26′N 70°23′E); Simpson's (1881) Nagarahara named from it
evidence: Colonel Jenkins' tunnel of 1878, 9 m into the square base, found only a stray bronze coin of Apollodotus I or II in the spoil. Simpson cleared part of one side: base c. 36.6 m square, dome c. 30.5 m diameter, stairs as at Ahinposh, a boulder core with radiating masonry ribs; c. 6 m in, a wall across the tunnel, which Simpson thought circular, suggests an earlier core stupa encased in the later enlargement. No relic deposit recorded.
quote: His tunnel 9m into the square base unearthed a stray bronze … tunnel’, which Simpson thought was circular. This suggests … the existence of an earlier core stupa encased within the later
note: Site data for Watters' candidate (after Masson and Simpson) in the study's open 02.03.02: a large stupa with an earlier core, but undated (the Apollodotus coin is a stray) and nothing ties it to Dīpaṅkara; Simpson's choice of it rests on the name. Leaves the place open.

author: Errington
name_in_asr: Ahinposh / Ahin Push / Ayun Posh / Ahunpok
asr_identification: Ahinposh stupa and monastery on a hill c. 2 km S of Jalalabad, W of the Hadda road (Ball and Gardin no. 17: 34°24′N 70°27′E)
evidence: Simpson's excavation, February 1879: stupa base 35 m square, podium 30.5 m square with 14 pilasters a side, dome c. 24.4 m diameter, Indo-Corinthian capitals, stairs N and S (E and W projections added later), five stucco Buddhas in situ on the W side; courtyard gate with the feet of a colossal image. Central relic cell 40 cm square of slate slabs, c. 3.65 m above ground, holding ashes, a gold amulet case with garnets and 18 gold coins: Wima Kadphises (10), Kanishka I (6), Huvishka (1) and Roman aurei of Domitian, Trajan and Sabina (AD 90–137). The deposit belongs to the Kushan period (Huvishka c. AD 150–90).
quote: This contained a small relic cell, 40cm square, the sides … held two handfuls of ‘brown dust’, possibly ashes, 18 gold … coins and an amulet case … Fig. 223), Wardak 1 and Ahinposh (the last with Roman … gold aurei of AD 90–137: see Fig. 242).
note: Excavation data for the Foucher/Higuchi candidate (Mizutani's 'possibly') in 02.03.02; Errington does not tie Ahinposh to Dīpaṅkara. The deposit dates the stupa (or its relic deposit) to the 2nd c. AD, as Foucher said from the same coins; it is not Aśokan, but Xuanzang's attribution need not be historical. Gives no ground to prefer it over Tepe Khwaja Lahori or Nagara Ghundi; the place stays open.

author: Errington
name_in_asr: Xuanzang's city; the 'shadow' of Buddha; Hi-lo / Hida
asr_identification: Masson (c. 1842–53, 'Caves of Jalalabad and Kabul', BL G41): the city in the plain of Jalalabad between the present town and Balabagh, possibly W of Jalalabad; Faxian's Hi-lo perhaps Hadda
evidence: Masson, working from Abel-Rémusat's Faxian (Julien's Xuanzang not yet out), argues the city lay in the plain of Jalalabad, perhaps W of the town, with the shadow 2 miles S of it; Faxian's Hi-lo 3 yojanas SE might be Hida = Hadda. From the coins in the relic deposits the topes are Kushan or later, so none can be shown to be Aśoka's stupa; the Darunta and Chahar Bagh groups predate Xuanzang, Hadda spans a longer period. Also equates Lan-po with Laghman at 100 li.
quote: These data should perhaps refer … rather to a city west of Jalalabad than to one at or near its site – … been in the actual plain of Jalalabad, and somewhere between the … could we fancy it by any chance to denote Hida, we should be … prone to connect it with the modern Hadda.
note: Agrees with the study (Begram plain; Hadda = 醯羅城); historically the first identification of Hi-lo with Hadda, before Cunningham, from Masson's unpublished treatise edited here. Adds no site evidence; Laghman = 02.02 likewise as the study.

author: Errington
asr_identification: Hadda 10 (Tope Kelan), Hadda, S of Jalalabad
evidence: The largest relic deposit Masson found: over 200 coins, mostly Sasanian silver of Varhran IV, Yazdagird II and Peroz (to AD 484), 5 Roman gold solidi of Theodosius II, Marcianus and Leo (AD 408–74), Alkhan Hun imitations and 14 Alkhan coins: the stupa was built and consecrated in the mid or late 5th century. Errington: substantial new stupas were still being built at Hadda in the late 5th century.
quote: The biggest relic deposit in the Masson collection is from … Hadda 10 (Tope Kelan; see Figs 278.39–43, 281–2). It … Sasanian coins provided a chronological context of the mid … or late 5th century, not only for the stupa, but also for the
note: Agrees with the study (Hadda secure). Errington does not connect it to Xuanzang, but a major new stupa dated mid/late 5th c. at Hadda fits Kuwayama's argument (note 02.03.05) that the skull relic and other relics were gathered at Hadda between the mid-5th c. and 629.

author: Errington
name_in_asr: skull bone relics at Hadda and Nagarahara
evidence: Cites Faxian and Xuanzang for the skull-bone relics; discusses skulls in Masson's Darunta tumuli and the Hadda Tepe Shotor meditation fresco; no site identification.

author: Errington
name_in_asr: Begram (Kohistan); Koh-i Bacha / Koh-i Top / Koh-i Pahlavan; Topdara; Shotorak; Qul-i Nadir; Paitava
asr_identification: Begram near Charikar (Kapisa province) and its stupas
evidence: Masson's records: Koh-i Bacha (= Koh-i Pahlavan) stupa at the E end of the ridge E of Burj Abdullah, 'the citadel' of Begram, with an earlier core stupa holding bones and ashes (Ball and Gardin no. 620, Ghundi Paisa), grouped with Shotorak and Qul-i Nadir further SE on the same ridge; Topdara 1 near Charikar, the largest extant stupa in Afghanistan, opened 1833 (only a bone fragment). Errington names no Xuanzang place in Kapisa.

note: No identification of Xiyu ji places in Kapisa; the site data are consistent with the study's Begram (01.38a), Koh-i Pahlavan (01.38.01) and Topdara (01.38.04) but do not test them.
